# Experiment Design: Does Bigger Necessarily Win? Llama-2 70B vs 13B Under Confounded Pre-Training and Alignment

---

## 0. Design-Only Statement

This document is a design specification. No models were loaded. No prompts were generated. No scores were computed. No statistical tests were performed. All numerical values for VRAM, API costs, and benchmark sizes are planning estimates drawn from published model cards and benchmark documentation. Nothing in this document is a result.

---

## 1. Research Question and What "Necessarily" Demands

**Question:** Does increasing model size (Llama-2-70B vs Llama-2-13B) *necessarily* yield improved performance, or can insufficient pre-training and a lack of refined alignment negate the benefits of a larger parameter count?

The word that drives the whole design is **"necessarily."** A comparison that shows 70B beats 13B on average does not answer the question. The question asks whether there exist conditions under which the 13B matches or beats the 70B, and if so, what those conditions are. Concretely, the analysis must terminate in a **conditional statement** of the form:

> Size (70B over 13B) yields improved performance on *k* of *m* tasks. It does **not** necessarily yield improvement when:
> - **(C1) Alignment negation:** the alignment gain at 13B (Δ_align_13B) is at least as large as the size gap at chat (Δ_size_chat) on alignment-sensitive tasks (Layer 3), so that 13B-chat matches or exceeds 70B-chat on those tasks; **or**
> - **(C2) Data-volume confound:** the 70B's pre-training advantage is attributable primarily to a larger training-token budget rather than to its 5.4× parameter count, as quantified by tokens-per-parameter.

The design is structured so that **both** conditions are tested, and the 2×2 mosaic (Section 7) is the figure that carries this conclusion.

---

## 2. Comparison Arms

Five arms. Arms A–D stay within the Llama-2 family (same tokenizer, same architecture family, same context window) so that parameter count and alignment are the only variables that change. Arm E deliberately breaks the family to isolate alignment.

| Arm | Models | What it isolates |
|-----|--------|-----------------|
| **A – Headline** | 70B-**chat** vs 13B-**chat** | The comparison the question asks about. Size + alignment, both active. |
| **B – Pre-training only** | 70B-**base** vs 13B-**base** | Size with alignment removed. If 70B-base still dominates, the gap is in pre-training / capacity, not in the alignment step. |
| **C – Alignment delta** | (70B-chat − 70B-base) vs (13B-chat − 13B-base) | How much each model *gains* from alignment. Tests whether alignment refinement is size-independent. |
| **D – Size-matched control** | 7B-**chat** vs 13B-**chat** | A smaller size step (7→13) against the larger step (13→70). If the proportional gap shrinks from 7→13 to 13→70, that is evidence of diminishing returns or under-training at the top end. |
| **E – Cross-alignment control** | 13B-**chat** vs a same-size model with a *different* alignment recipe (see fallback below) | Isolates "refined alignment" from "Llama-2 alignment." If a well-aligned 13B beats a 70B that received a cruder alignment pass on instruction tasks, alignment can negate size. |

**Arm E primary choice:** Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 (same size class, different architecture, different alignment recipe — DPO-based vs Llama-2's RLHF). This is a *size-matched, differently-aligned* control. The architecture difference is a limitation (it is not a pure alignment ablation), but it tests the practical question: "does a 13B-class model with a different alignment recipe close the gap to 70B?"

**Arm E fallback (locked in per researcher directive):** If no clean same-size, differently-aligned model is available at execution time, fall back to a **same-model, different-alignment ablation**: Llama-2-13B-chat vs Llama-2-13B-DPO (or any publicly available 13B fine-tune of Llama-2-base with a non-RLHF alignment method). This keeps the comparison within the same base model and architecture, isolating the alignment recipe as the only variable. If neither is available, Arm E is replaced by a sensitivity check: re-run Arm A with a different decoding temperature (0.3 vs 0.7) to test whether the 70B's advantage on generative tasks is an artifact of the decoding regime rather than a model property.

**Generative-task judge (pinned):** All LLM-as-judge evaluations (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval) use **GPT-4-2024-11-06** as the judge, called with temperature=0. The judge model, prompt template, and scoring rubric are fixed and versioned before any model is evaluated. No model is judged by itself. If GPT-4-2024-11-06 is unavailable, the fallback is GPT-4o-2024-08-06, and the switch is noted in the results. The judge is external to all evaluated models.

---

## 3. Benchmark Battery: Three Layers

The battery is split into three layers so that "performance" is decomposed into pre-training quality, reasoning capability, and alignment. Each model is evaluated on **identical prompts** with **identical decoding parameters**.

### Layer 1: Pre-Training / Knowledge

Measures raw capacity and data exposure. These are the tasks most sensitive to "insufficient pre-training."

| Task | Format | Sample size | Decoding | Metric |
|------|--------|-------------|----------|--------|
| C4 validation perplexity | Left-to-right NLL, 10K-token fixed sample | 10,000 tokens | n/a (no generation) | PPL (lower is better) |
| WikiText-103 test perplexity | Same protocol | 10,000 tokens | n/a | PPL |
| MMLU | 5-shot multiple choice, 4 options | 2,000 questions (stratified by subject) | temperature=0, max_new_tokens=8 | Accuracy (%) |
| TriviaQA | 5-shot short answer | 1,000 questions | temperature=0, max_new_tokens=32 | Exact-match accuracy (%) |

### Layer 2: Reasoning / Capability

Measures whether extra parameters buy actual reasoning ability, not just pattern matching.

| Task | Format | Sample size | Decoding | Metric |
|------|--------|-------------|----------|--------|
| GSM8K | 5-shot, grade-school math | 1,319 problems (full test set) | temperature=0, max_new_tokens=512 | Exact-match accuracy (%) |
| MATH | 4-shot, competition math | 1,000 problems (stratified by topic) | temperature=0, max_new_tokens=1024 | Exact-match accuracy (%) |
| ARC-Challenge | 25-shot multiple choice | 1,172 problems (full test set) | temperature=0, max_new_tokens=8 | Accuracy (%) |
| HellaSwag | 10-shot commonsense | 2,000 examples (validation split) | temperature=0, max_new_tokens=8 | Accuracy (%) |
| Winogrande | 5-shot coreference | 1,267 problems (full test set) | temperature=0, max_new_tokens=8 | Accuracy (%) |

### Layer 3: Alignment / Instruction

Measures "refined alignment." These are the tasks where a well-aligned smaller model can plausibly match or beat a larger model.

| Task | Format | Sample size | Decoding | Metric |
|------|--------|-------------|----------|--------|
| MT-Bench | 8 categories × 10 questions × 2 turns | 160 prompts | temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, max_new_tokens=1024, **3 seeds** | GPT-4-2024-11-06 score (1–10), mean across seeds |
| AlpacaEval 2.0 | 805 instructions, win rate vs GPT-4-0613 reference | 805 prompts | temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, max_new_tokens=2048, **3 seeds** | Win rate (%), mean across seeds |
| IFEval | 500 instruction-following prompts with verifiable constraints | 500 prompts | temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, max_new_tokens=1024, **3 seeds** | Strict accuracy (%) — all constraints met |
| Harmlessness | 200 adversarial / jailbreak prompts | 200 prompts | temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, max_new_tokens=512, **3 seeds** | Refusal rate (%) + 50-sample human spot-check |

**Total prompts per model:** approximately 11,000–12,000 (including 3 seeds for Layer 3).
**Total prompts across all models (6 Llama-2 variants + 1–2 cross-family):** approximately 75,000–85,000.

### Decoding parameter summary

- **Objective tasks (Layers 1–2):** temperature=0, top_p=1.0, max_new_tokens as specified. One pass per prompt (greedy decoding is deterministic).
- **Generative tasks (Layer 3):** temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, max_new_tokens as specified. **Three independent seeds** per prompt to estimate output variance. The reported score is the mean across seeds.
- **Perplexity:** standard left-to-right tokenization, no generation. The 10K-token sample is identical across all models.

---

## 4. Variable Isolation Strategy

### 4a. Primary Axis: Capacity Under-Training (Interpretation 1)

**Spine (per researcher directive):** The primary interpretation of "insufficient pre-training" is that the 70B model's parameter capacity is not fully utilized by its training budget. In other words, a 70B model needs more training tokens to reach the same quality-per-parameter as a 13B model, and if it was trained on the same or proportionally fewer tokens, it is under-trained relative to its capacity.

**How the design tests this:**

1. **Arm B (base-vs-base) + Layer 1 perplexity.** Compute PPL on C4 and WikiText-103 for 7B-base, 13B-base, and 70B-base. If the 70B-base PPL is not proportionally better than the 13B-base PPL (e.g., the PPL ratio 70B/13B is close to 1.0 when the parameter ratio is 5.4×), the 70B is under-trained relative to its capacity. The specific test: compute ΔPPL = PPL(13B-base) − PPL(70B-base). If ΔPPL is small relative to the parameter ratio, the 70B's extra parameters are not translating into proportionally better language modeling.

2. **Arm D (7B vs 13B) as a scaling check.** If the 7B→13B PPL improvement is *larger* (in absolute terms) than the 13B→70B PPL improvement, that is evidence of diminishing returns: the 70B is not getting as much benefit from its extra parameters as the 13B got from its extra parameters over the 7B.

3. **Tokens-per-parameter (see 4b).** This is the quantitative backing.

### 4b. Secondary Axis: Token-Budget Confound (Interpretation 2)

**Reported via tokens-per-parameter, not as a separate experiment.** If the 13B and 70B were trained on different total token counts, the "size" comparison is confounded with "data volume." The design reports:

- **tokens_per_param(model) = total_training_tokens / num_parameters** for each model.
- The ratio: tokens_per_param(70B) / tokens_per_param(13B).
- If this ratio is close to 1.0, the two models were trained on proportional token budgets and the size comparison is clean.
- If this ratio is substantially less than 1.0 (e.g., the 70B got 2.0T tokens for 70B params = 28.6K tokens/param, while the 13B got 1.0T tokens for 13B params = 76.9K tokens/param), the 13B was actually trained on *3× more tokens per parameter*, and the "size advantage" of the 70B is confounded by the fact that the 13B saw more data per parameter.

This number is reported in every results table and in the 2×2 mosaic. It does not change the experimental arms, but it changes the *interpretation* of Arm A and Arm B results.

### 4c. Alignment Isolation

- **Arm C** directly computes the alignment delta at each size: Δ_align_13B = score(13B-chat) − score(13B-base), Δ_align_70B = score(70B-chat) − score(70B-base). The key comparison is the ratio Δ_align_13B / Δ_align_70B. If this ratio ≥ 1.0 on Layer 3 tasks, alignment helps the smaller model at least as much, and the size gap on alignment tasks can be closed.
- **Arm E** tests whether a *different* alignment recipe at 13B scale can close the gap to 70B. This is the most direct test of "can a lack of refined alignment negate the benefits of a larger parameter count?"

---

## 5. Training Token Budgets (A1)

**Values recalled from the Llama-2 technical report (Touvron et al., 2023, arXiv:2307.09288), Table 1 / training section:**

| Model | Training tokens (recalled) | Parameters | Tokens/param (derived) |
|-------|---------------------------|------------|----------------------|
| Llama-2-7B | 2.0T | 6.7B | ~299K |
| Llama-2-13B | 1.0T | 13.0B | ~76.9K |
| Llama-2-70B | 2.0T | 70.0B | ~28.6K |

**These values are from memory and have NOT been verified in this session.** The network is disabled and the paper is not in the workspace. Before execution, the token counts must be confirmed from the published paper. If the 13B was actually trained on 2.0T tokens (not 1.0T), the tokens-per-parameter ratio between 13B and 70B is approximately 1.0, and Interpretation 2 (data-volume confound) collapses — the size comparison is clean and the analysis focuses entirely on Interpretation 1 (capacity under-training).

**This is the single most important number to verify before running the experiment.** The entire narrative shifts depending on whether the 13B saw 1.0T or 2.0T tokens.

---

## 6. Analysis Plan

### 6a. Per-Task Metrics

For each task, each model, the following are computed:

- **Objective tasks (Layers 1–2):** accuracy (%) or PPL. One value per model (greedy decoding is deterministic).
- **Generative tasks (Layer 3):** mean score across 3 seeds, with standard deviation across seeds. The 3-seed SD is the within-model variance.

### 6b. Statistical Tests

**Primary comparison (Arm A): 70B-chat vs 13B-chat**

- For objective tasks: paired comparison on per-problem scores. Compute the paired difference d_i = score_70B(problem_i) − score_13B(problem_i) for each problem. Report:
  - Mean of d_i (the point estimate of the size effect)
  - 95% confidence interval via **10,000-pair bootstrap resampling** of the d_i values
  - Cohen's d (paired) as the effect size: d = mean(d_i) / SD(d_i)
  - The bootstrap 95% CI is the primary inferential tool. We do not rely on a single p-value.

- For generative tasks (Layer 3): the comparison is more complex because each (model, problem) pair has 3 seed-level scores. Use a **linear mixed-effects model**:
  - Fixed effects: model (70B vs 13B), task
  - Random intercept: problem (to account for repeated measures across models)
  - Outcome: per-seed score
  - Report the fixed-effect coefficient for model with 95% CI (profile-likelihood or Wald, whichever is more stable for small n)
  - If the mixed model is unstable (n_problems < 50 for a given task), fall back to a paired t-test on the 3-seed means per problem, with the 95% CI from the t-distribution.

**Secondary comparisons (Arms B, C, D, E):** same tests, applied to the relevant model pairs.

**Multiple testing correction:** Across the 14 tasks in the battery, apply **Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction** (q = 0.05) to the set of p-values from the primary (Arm A) comparisons. Report both raw and FDR-adjusted CIs. The FDR-corrected result is the one used for the "necessarily" conclusion.

### 6c. The 2×2 Mosaic (Centerpiece Figure)

This is the figure that carries the conclusion. It is a 2×2 grid:

```
                    Base (no alignment)              Chat (aligned)
                ┌──────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────┐
  13B           │  13B-base                 │   │  13B-chat                │
                │  Mean score: X₁ (CI: ...) │   │  Mean score: X₂ (CI: ...)│
                │  PPL: x₁                  │   │  PPL: x₂                 │
                └──────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────────┘
                ┌──────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────┐
  70B           │  70B-base                 │   │  70B-chat                │
                │  Mean score: X₃ (CI: ...) │   │  Mean score: X₄ (CI: ...)│
                │  PPL: x₃                  │   │  PPL: x₄                 │
                └──────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────────┘
```

**Each cell contains:**
- Mean score across the 3-layer battery, with 95% CI (bootstrap, 10K resamples)
- Layer-specific scores (L1, L2, L3) as separate rows within the cell
- PPL on C4 and WikiText-103 (from Layer 1)

**The four comparisons drawn on the mosaic:**

| Comparison | Computation | What it tells us |
|-----------|-------------|-----------------|
| **Δ_size_base** (vertical, left column) | X₃ − X₁ | Size effect with no alignment. Pure pre-training / capacity. |
| **Δ_size_chat** (vertical, right column) | X₄ − X₂ | Size effect with alignment. The headline number. |
| **Δ_align_13B** (horizontal, top row) | X₂ − X₁ | How much the 13B gains from alignment. |
| **Δ_align_70B** (horizontal, bottom row) | X₄ − X₃ | How much the 70B gains from alignment. |

**The "necessarily" test, read from the mosaic:**

- If Δ_size_chat > 0 (95% CI excludes 0) on **all 14 tasks**, size necessarily yields improvement (within the limits of this benchmark battery).
- If Δ_size_chat ≤ 0 (or 95% CI includes 0) on **any task**, size does **not** necessarily yield improvement. The specific tasks where this happens are the answer to the question.
- **Condition C1 (alignment negation) is met** if Δ_align_13B ≥ Δ_size_chat on any Layer 3 task. In the mosaic, this means the top-row horizontal arrow is at least as long as the right-column vertical arrow, for that task.
- **Condition C2 (data-volume confound) is met** if tokens_per_param(70B) / tokens_per_param(13B) < 0.5 (i.e., the 70B got less than half the tokens per parameter of the 13B). This is a property of the training, not of the mosaic, but it is annotated on the figure.

**The mosaic is reported at three levels of aggregation:**
1. **Overall battery mean** (all 14 tasks averaged) — the headline number.
2. **Per-layer means** (L1, L2, L3) — shows where the size effect is strong and where it disappears.
3. **Per-task** (14 individual cells) — the full detail, in a supplementary table.

### 6d. Decomposition Regression

Fit a linear model across all model-task observations:

```
task_score = β₀ + β₁·log10(params) + β₂·log10(tokens_per_param) + β₃·is_aligned + β₄·task_layer + ε
```

- `task_score`: the model's score on a given task (standardized to z-scores across tasks to make them comparable).
- `log10(params)`: 7B=9.83, 13B=10.11, 70B=10.85 (log10 of parameter count).
- `log10(tokens_per_param)`: from Section 5.
- `is_aligned`: 0 for base, 1 for chat.
- `task_layer`: 1, 2, or 3.

**What this gives us:**
- β₁: the partial effect of parameter count, holding tokens-per-param and alignment constant. If β₁ is small or non-significant after controlling for tokens_per_param, the "size" effect is mostly a data-volume effect.
- β₂: the partial effect of training data density. If β₂ is large and β₁ is small, the 70B's advantage is mostly "it saw more data per parameter" (or "the 13B saw more data per parameter," depending on which interpretation of the token counts is correct).
- β₃: the alignment effect, holding size and data constant. If β₃ is large and comparable to β₁, alignment is as important as size.

This regression is a **descriptive decomposition**, not a causal claim. It is reported with 95% CIs on all coefficients and is interpreted alongside the 2×2 mosaic, not instead of it.

### 6e. Effect-Size Framing

- **Primary:** mean difference + 95% CI (bootstrap, 10K resamples). This is the number reported in every table and the mosaic.
- **Secondary:** Cohen's d (paired) for objective tasks. Reported alongside the CI.
- **Tertiary:** for generative tasks, the between-model SD / within-model (across-seed) SD ratio. If the between-model difference is smaller than the within-model seed variance, the "effect" is not reliable at the individual-prompt level.
- **No bare p-values.** Every claim in the results section is of the form: "70B-chat scored X% higher than 13B-chat on GSM8K (95% CI [a, b], paired bootstrap, n=1319, Cohen's d = c)."

## 7. Feasibility

### 7a. Concrete Compute Costs

**Model weights (inference, not training):**

| Model | fp16 VRAM | int8 VRAM | int4 (GPTQ/AWQ) VRAM |
|-------|-----------|-----------|----------------------|
| 7B | 13.4 GB | 6.7 GB | 3.4 GB |
| 13B | 26.0 GB | 13.0 GB | 6.5 GB |
| 70B | 140.0 GB | 70.0 GB | 35.0 GB |

**Hardware options for 70B inference:**
- **fp16:** 2× A100-80GB (160 GB total) or 2× H100-80GB. Minimum 2 GPUs.
- **int8:** 1× A100-80GB (70 GB weights + ~10 GB KV cache for 4K context = 80 GB, tight but feasible).
- **int4 (GPTQ or AWQ):** 1× A100-40GB or 1× H100-80GB with room to spare. Quantization introduces a small accuracy penalty (~0.5–1.5% on objective tasks, per published GPTQ papers), which is acceptable for a design-validation pilot but should be noted if used in the full run.
- **API:** No local GPU needed. Llama-2 models are available via Together AI, Fireworks AI, or self-hosted vLLM endpoints.

**API cost estimate (full evaluation, all arms, all seeds):**

| Item | Estimate |
|------|----------|
| Total prompts (all models, all seeds) | ~80,000 |
| Average tokens per prompt (input + output) | ~500 |
| Total tokens | ~40M |
| 70B at ~$2.00/M tokens (Together AI) | ~$80 |
| 13B at ~$0.40/M tokens | ~$16 |
| 7B at ~$0.15/M tokens | ~$6 |
| Cross-family (Mistral-7B or 13B-DPO) | ~$10 |
| GPT-4-2024-11-06 judge (Layer 3, ~10K judge calls) | ~$50–100 |
| **Total API cost** | **~$160–210** |

This is a rough estimate. Actual costs depend on the provider, token counts, and retry rates. The order of magnitude is **low hundreds of dollars**, not thousands.

**GPU cost estimate (if self-hosted):**
- 70B on 2× A100-80GB: ~200–400 GPU-hours for the full evaluation (80K prompts, 70B is the bottleneck at ~50–100 tokens/sec on 2× A100). At $3–5/GPU-hour on a cloud provider: **~$1,200–4,000**.
- 13B on 1× A100-80GB: ~50–100 GPU-hours: **~$300–500**.
- 7B on 1× A100-40GB: ~20–40 GPU-hours: **~$100–200**.
- **Total GPU cost: ~$1,600–4,700.**

API is roughly 10× cheaper than self-hosted GPU for this workload.

### 7b. Staged Fallback (Locked In)

The experiment is executed in two stages to de-risk the harness before committing 70B compute:

**Stage 1 – Pilot (7B vs 13B, all 3 layers):**
- Evaluate 7B-base, 7B-chat, 13B-base, 13B-chat on the full 14-task battery.
- 4 models × ~12K prompts = ~48K prompts.
- All 4 models fit in fp16 on a single A100-80GB (7B: 13.4 GB, 13B: 26.0 GB).
- **Purpose:** validate the evaluation pipeline (prompt formatting, decoding parameters, scoring functions, bootstrap CI code, mixed-model fitting, judge API calls). Catch bugs before the 70B run.
- **Cost:** ~$50–100 (API) or ~$400–600 (GPU).
- **Success criteria for proceeding to Stage 2:** all 14 tasks produce finite scores for all 4 models; the bootstrap CI code produces expected CIs on a synthetic test; the judge API returns valid scores for all Layer 3 prompts.

**Stage 2 – Full (add 70B, all 5 arms):**
- Add 70B-base and 70B-chat to the evaluation.
- Run Arm E (cross-family or ablation).
- Full 6–7 models × ~12K prompts = ~80K prompts.
- **Cost:** ~$100–150 additional (API) or ~$1,200–4,000 additional (GPU).
- **This is the run that produces the 2×2 mosaic and the "necessarily" conclusion.**

**Stage 3 – Sensitivity (optional, if time/compute allows):**
- Re-run Layer 3 with temperature=0.3 (instead of 0.7) to test whether the alignment results are temperature-sensitive.
- Add a second cross-family model to Arm E if the first one has issues.
- Human evaluation on a 100-prompt subset of Layer 3 to check judge agreement (Cohen's κ between GPT-4 judge and human raters).

### 7c. Design-Only Restatement

This document specifies what to run, how to run it, and how to analyze the results. **Nothing described here was executed in the preparation of this document.** The workspace contains no model weights, no datasets, no inference code, and no GPU. All costs and timings are planning estimates.

---

| **A1** | Training token counts: 7B=2.0T, 13B=1.0T, 70B=2.0T. **Recalled from the Llama-2 paper, not verified in this session.** | **Unverified assumption.** Must confirm from arXiv:2307.09288 before execution. | If 13B was actually 2.0T, the tokens-per-param ratio is ~1.0, Interpretation 2 collapses, and the analysis is purely about capacity under-training. |

| **A7** | GPT-4-2024-11-06 is available as the external judge for Layer 3. Fallback: GPT-4o-2024-08-06. | Assumed available. | If neither is available, Layer 3 LLM-judge tasks (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval) must be replaced with human-rated subsets (100–200 prompts, 2 raters, Cohen's κ reported). |
| **A8** | Quantization (if used for 70B on a single GPU) introduces ≤1.5% accuracy loss on objective tasks. | Assumed from published GPTQ/AWQ papers. | If the quantization penalty is larger, 70B scores are slightly depressed and the size gap is underestimated. Report quantization method and level in the results. |

---

## 9. What This Design Can and Cannot Tell Us

**Can tell us:**
- Whether 70B-chat beats 13B-chat on each of 14 specific tasks, with a 95% CI.
- Whether the 70B's advantage is uniform across task types or concentrated in pre-training / reasoning (Layers 1–2) and absent in alignment (Layer 3).
- How much of the 70B's advantage is attributable to parameter count vs. training data volume (via tokens-per-parameter and the decomposition regression).
- How much each model gains from alignment (Arm C), and whether that gain is size-dependent.
- Whether a differently-aligned 13B-class model can close the gap to 70B on instruction tasks (Arm E).
- A conditional answer to "necessarily": the specific tasks and conditions under which size does *not* yield improvement.

**Cannot tell us (without additional experiments):**
- Whether a *retrained* 70B with more tokens would perform better (we cannot retrain; we can only measure the published checkpoints).
- Whether the 70B's alignment is "less refined" than the 13B's in an absolute sense, or whether both are well-aligned and the difference is in base-model quality.
- Causal claims about *why* the 70B performs as it does (the decomposition regression is descriptive, not causal).
- Generalization beyond the Llama-2 family and the specific benchmarks in the battery.

---

## 10. Summary of the Design in One Paragraph

We evaluate six Llama-2 variants (7B/13B/70B × base/chat) plus one cross-family or same-model-different-alignment control on a 14-task battery spanning pre-training quality (PPL, MMLU, TriviaQA), reasoning (GSM8K, MATH, ARC, HellaSwag, Winogrande), and alignment (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval, IFEval, harmlessness). The centerpiece is a 2×2 mosaic (size × alignment) that reports the mean score and 95% CI in each cell, with the four inter-cell differences (Δ_size_base, Δ_size_chat, Δ_align_13B, Δ_align_70B) annotated. The primary statistical test is a paired bootstrap (10K resamples) on per-problem scores, with FDR correction across tasks. ## 1. Research Question and What "Necessarily" Demands

**Question:** Does increasing model size (Llama-2-70B vs Llama-2-13B) *necessarily* yield improved performance, or can insufficient pre-training and a lack of refined alignment negate the benefits of a larger parameter count?

The word that drives the whole design is **"necessarily."** A comparison that shows 70B beats 13B on average does not answer the question. The question asks whether there exist conditions under which the 13B matches or beats the 70B, and if so, what those conditions are. The design is structured so that **both** conditions are tested, and the 2×2 mosaic (Section 7) is the figure that carries this conclusion.

## 4. Variable Isolation Strategy

### 4a. Primary Axis: Capacity Under-Training (Interpretation 1)

**Spine (per researcher directive):** The primary interpretation of "insufficient pre-training" is that the 70B model's parameter capacity is not fully utilized by its training budget. In other words, a 70B model needs more training tokens to reach the same quality-per-parameter as a 13B model, and if it was trained on the same or proportionally fewer tokens, it is under-trained relative to its capacity.

**How the design tests this:**

1. **Arm B (base-vs-base) + Layer 1 perplexity.** Compute PPL on C4 and WikiText-103 for 7B-base, 13B-base, and 70B-base. If the 70B-base PPL is not proportionally better than the 13B-base PPL (e.g., the PPL ratio 70B/13B is close to 1.0 when the parameter ratio is 5.4×), the 70B is under-trained relative to its capacity. The specific test: compute ΔPPL = PPL(13B-base) − PPL(70B-base). If ΔPPL is small relative to the parameter ratio, the 70B's extra parameters are not translating into proportionally better language modeling.

2. **Arm D (7B vs 13B) as a scaling check.** If the 7B→13B PPL improvement is *larger* (in absolute terms) than the 13B→70B PPL improvement, that is evidence of diminishing returns: the 70B is not getting as much benefit from its extra parameters as the 13B got from its extra parameters over the 7B.

3. **Tokens-per-parameter (see 4b).** This is the quantitative backing.

### 4b. Secondary Axis: Token-Budget Confound (Interpretation 2)

**Reported via tokens-per-parameter, not as a separate experiment.** If the 13B and 70B were trained on different total token counts, the "size" comparison is confounded with "data volume." The design reports:

- **tokens_per_param(model) = total_training_tokens / num_parameters** for each model.
- The ratio: tokens_per_param(70B) / tokens_per_param(13B).
- If this ratio is close to 1.0, the two models were trained on proportional token budgets and the size comparison is clean.
- If this ratio is substantially less than 1.0 (e.g., the 70B got 2.0T tokens for 70B params = 28.6K tokens/param, while the 13B got 1.0T tokens for 13B params = 76.9K tokens/param), the 13B was actually trained on *3× more tokens per parameter*, and the "size advantage" of the 70B is confounded by the fact that the 13B saw more data per parameter.

This number is reported in every results table and in the 2×2 mosaic. It does not change the experimental arms, but it changes the *interpretation* of Arm A and Arm B results.

### 4c. Alignment Isolation

- **Arm C** directly computes the alignment delta at each size: Δ_align_13B = score(13B-chat) − score(13B-base), Δ_align_70B = score(70B-chat) − score(70B-base). The key comparison is the ratio Δ_align_13B / Δ_align_70B. If this ratio ≥ 1.0 on Layer 3 tasks, alignment helps the smaller model at least as much, and the size gap on alignment tasks can be closed.
- **Arm E** tests whether a *different* alignment recipe at 13B scale can close the gap to 70B. This is the most direct test of "can a lack of refined alignment negate the benefits of a larger parameter count?"

## 6. Analysis Plan

### 6a. Per-Task Metrics

For each task, each model, the following are computed:

- **Objective tasks (Layers 1–2):** accuracy (%) or PPL. One value per model (greedy decoding is deterministic).
- **Generative tasks (Layer 3):** mean score across 3 seeds, with standard deviation across seeds. The 3-seed SD is the within-model variance.

### 6b. Statistical Tests

**Primary comparison (Arm A): 70B-chat vs 13B-chat**

- For objective tasks: paired comparison on per-problem scores. Compute the paired difference d_i = score_70B(problem_i) − score_13B(problem_i) for each problem. Report:
  - Mean of d_i (the point estimate of the size effect)
  - 95% confidence interval via **10,000-pair bootstrap resampling** of the d_i values
  - Cohen's d (paired) as the effect size: d = mean(d_i) / SD(d_i)
  - The bootstrap 95% CI is the primary inferential tool. We do not rely on a single p-value.

- For generative tasks (Layer 3): the comparison is more complex because each (model, problem) pair has 3 seed-level scores. Use a **linear mixed-effects model**:
  - Fixed effects: model (70B vs 13B), task
  - Random intercept: problem (to account for repeated measures across models)
  - Outcome: per-seed score
  - Report the fixed-effect coefficient for model with 95% CI (profile-likelihood or Wald, whichever is more stable for small n)
  - If the mixed model is unstable (n_problems < 50 for a given task), fall back to a paired t-test on the 3-seed means per problem, with the 95% CI from the t-distribution.

**Secondary comparisons (Arms B, C, D, E):** same tests, applied to the relevant model pairs.

**Multiple testing correction:** Across the 14 tasks in the battery, apply **Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction** (q = 0.05) to the set of p-values from the primary (Arm A) comparisons. Report both raw and FDR-adjusted CIs. The FDR-corrected result is the one used for the "necessarily" conclusion.

**The four comparisons drawn on the mosaic:**

| Comparison | Computation | What it tells us |
|-----------|-------------|-----------------|

**The "necessarily" test, read from the mosaic:**

- If Δ_size_chat > 0 (95% CI excludes 0) on **all 14 tasks**, size necessarily yields improvement (within the limits of this benchmark battery).
- If Δ_size_chat ≤ 0 (or 95% CI includes 0) on **any task**, size does **not** necessarily yield improvement. The specific tasks where this happens are the answer to the question.
- **Condition C1 (alignment negation) is met** if Δ_align_13B ≥ Δ_size_chat on any Layer 3 task. In the mosaic, this means the top-row horizontal arrow is at least as long as the right-column vertical arrow, for that task.
- **Condition C2 (data-volume confound) is met** if tokens_per_param(70B) / tokens_per_param(13B) < 0.5 (i.e., the 70B got less than half the tokens per parameter of the 13B). This is a property of the training, not of the mosaic, but it is annotated on the figure.

**The mosaic is reported at three levels of aggregation:**
1. **Overall battery mean** (all 14 tasks averaged) — the headline number.
2. **Per-layer means** (L1, L2, L3) — shows where the size effect is strong and where it disappears.
3. **Per-task** (14 individual cells) — the full detail, in a supplementary table.

### 6d. Decomposition Regression

Fit a linear model across all model-task observations:

```
task_score = β₀ + β₁·log10(params) + β₂·log10(tokens_per_param) + β₃·is_aligned + β₄·task_layer + ε
```

- `task_score`: the model's score on a given task (standardized to z-scores across tasks to make them comparable).
- `log10(params)`: 7B=9.83, 13B=10.11, 70B=10.85 (log10 of parameter count).
- `log10(tokens_per_param)`: from Section 5.
- `is_aligned`: 0 for base, 1 for chat.
- `task_layer`: 1, 2, or 3.

**What this gives us:**
- β₁: the partial effect of parameter count, holding tokens-per-param and alignment constant. If β₁ is small or non-significant after controlling for tokens_per_param, the "size" effect is mostly a data-volume effect.
- β₂: the partial effect of training data density. If β₂ is large and β₁ is small, the 70B's advantage is mostly "it saw more data per parameter" (or "the 13B saw more data per parameter," depending on which interpretation of the token counts is correct).
- β₃: the alignment effect, holding size and data constant. If β₃ is large and comparable to β₁, alignment is as important as size.

This regression is a **descriptive decomposition**, not a causal claim. It is reported with 95% CIs on all coefficients and is interpreted alongside the 2×2 mosaic, not instead of it.

### 6e. Effect-Size Framing

- **Primary:** mean difference + 95% CI (bootstrap, 10K resamples). This is the number reported in every table and the mosaic.
- **Secondary:** Cohen's d (paired) for objective tasks. Reported alongside the CI.
- **Tertiary:** for generative tasks, the between-model SD / within-model (across-seed) SD ratio. If the between-model difference is smaller than the within-model seed variance, the "effect" is not reliable at the individual-prompt level.
- **No bare p-values.** Every claim in the results section is of the form: "70B-chat scored X% higher than 13B-chat on GSM8K (95% CI [a, b], paired bootstrap, n=1319, Cohen's d = c)."

### 7b. Staged Fallback (Locked In)

The experiment is executed in two stages to de-risk the harness before committing 70B compute:

**Stage 1 – Pilot (7B vs 13B, all 3 layers):**
- Evaluate 7B-base, 7B-chat, 13B-base, 13B-chat on the full 14-task battery.
- 4 models × ~12K prompts = ~48K prompts.
- All 4 models fit in fp16 on a single A100-80GB (7B: 13.4 GB, 13B: 26.0 GB).
- **Purpose:** validate the evaluation pipeline (prompt formatting, decoding parameters, scoring functions, bootstrap CI code, mixed-model fitting, judge API calls). Catch bugs before the 70B run.
- **Cost:** ~$50–100 (API) or ~$400–600 (GPU).
- **Success criteria for proceeding to Stage 2:** all 14 tasks produce finite scores for all 4 models; the bootstrap CI code produces expected CIs on a synthetic test; the judge API returns valid scores for all Layer 3 prompts.

**Stage 2 – Full (add 70B, all 5 arms):**
- Add 70B-base and 70B-chat to the evaluation.
- Run Arm E (cross-family or ablation).
- Full 6–7 models × ~12K prompts = ~80K prompts.
- **Cost:** ~$100–150 additional (API) or ~$1,200–4,000 additional (GPU).
- **This is the run that produces the 2×2 mosaic and the "necessarily" conclusion.**

**Stage 3 – Sensitivity (optional, if time/compute allows):**
- Re-run Layer 3 with temperature=0.3 (instead of 0.7) to test whether the alignment results are temperature-sensitive.
- Add a second cross-family model to Arm E if the first one has issues.
- Human evaluation on a 100-prompt subset of Layer 3 to check judge agreement (Cohen's κ between GPT-4 judge and human raters).

## 9. What This Design Can and Cannot Tell Us

**Can tell us:**
- Whether 70B-chat beats 13B-chat on each of 14 specific tasks, with a 95% CI.
- Whether the 70B's advantage is uniform across task types or concentrated in pre-training / reasoning (Layers 1–2) and absent in alignment (Layer 3).
- How much of the 70B's advantage is attributable to parameter count vs. training data volume (via tokens-per-parameter and the decomposition regression).
- How much each model gains from alignment (Arm C), and whether that gain is size-dependent.
- Whether a differently-aligned 13B-class model can close the gap to 70B on instruction tasks (Arm E).
- A conditional answer to "necessarily": the specific tasks and conditions under which size does *not* yield improvement.

**Cannot tell us (without additional experiments):**
- Whether a *retrained* 70B with more tokens would perform better (we cannot retrain; we can only measure the published checkpoints).
- Whether the 70B's alignment is "less refined" than the 13B's in an absolute sense, or whether both are well-aligned and the difference is in base-model quality.
- Causal claims about *why* the 70B performs as it does (the decomposition regression is descriptive, not causal).
- Generalization beyond the Llama-2 family and the specific benchmarks in the battery.

Research Question and What \"Necessarily\" Demands\n\n**Question:** Does increasing model size (Llama-2-70B vs Llama-2-13B) *necessarily* yield improved performance, or can insufficient pre-training and a lack of refined alignment negate the benefits of a larger parameter count?\n\nThe word that drives the whole design is **\"necessarily.\"** A comparison that shows 70B beats 13B on average does not answer the question. The question asks whether there exist conditions under which the 13B matches or beats the 70B, and if so, what those conditions are. Concretely, the analysis must terminate in a **conditional statement** of the form:\n\n> Size (70B over 13B) yields improved performance on *k* of *m* tasks. It does **not** necessarily yield improvement when:\n> - **(C1) Alignment negation:** the alignment gain at 13B (\u0394_align_13B) is at least as large as the size gap at chat (\u0394_size_chat) on alignment-sensitive tasks (Layer 3), so that 13B-chat matches or exceeds 70B-chat on those tasks; **or**\n> - **(C2) Data-volume confound:** the 70B's pre-training advantage is attributable primarily to a larger training-token budget rather than to its 5.4\u00d7 parameter count, as quantified by tokens-per-parameter.\n\nThe design is structured so that **both** conditions are tested, and the 2\u00d72 mosaic (Section 7) is the figure that carries this conclusion.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Variable Isolation Strategy\n\n### 4a. Primary Axis: Capacity Under-Training (Interpretation 1)\n\n**Spine (per researcher directive):** The primary interpretation of \"insufficient pre-training\" is that the 70B model's parameter capacity is not fully utilized by its training budget. In other words, a 70B model needs more training tokens to reach the same quality-per-parameter as a 13B model, and if it was trained on the same or proportionally fewer tokens, it is under-trained relative to its capacity.\n\n**How the design tests this:**\n\n1. **Arm B (base-vs-base) + Layer 1 perplexity.** Compute PPL on C4 and WikiText-103 for 7B-base, 13B-base, and 70B-base. If the 70B-base PPL is not proportionally better than the 13B-base PPL (e.g., the PPL ratio 70B/13B is close to 1.0 when the parameter ratio is 5.4\u00d7), the 70B is under-trained relative to its capacity. The specific test: compute \u0394PPL = PPL(13B-base) \u2212 PPL(70B-base). If \u0394PPL is small relative to the parameter ratio, the 70B's extra parameters are not translating into proportionally better language modeling.\n\n2. **Arm D (7B vs 13B) as a scaling check.** If the 7B\u219213B PPL improvement is *larger* (in absolute terms) than the 13B\u219270B PPL improvement, that is evidence of diminishing returns: the 70B is not getting as much benefit from its extra parameters as the 13B got from its extra parameters over the 7B.\n\n3. **Tokens-per-parameter (see 4b).** This is the quantitative backing.\n\n### 4b. Secondary Axis: Token-Budget Confound (Interpretation 2)\n\n**Reported via tokens-per-parameter, not as a separate experiment.** If the 13B and 70B were trained on different total token counts, the \"size\" comparison is confounded with \"data volume.\" The design reports:\n\n- **tokens_per_param(model) = total_training_tokens / num_parameters** for each model.\n- The ratio: tokens_per_param(70B) / tokens_per_param(13B).\n- If this ratio is close to 1.0, the two models were trained on proportional token budgets and the size comparison is clean.\n- If this ratio is substantially less than 1.0 (e.g., the 70B got 2.0T tokens for 70B params = 28.6K tokens/param, while the 13B got 1.0T tokens for 13B params = 76.9K tokens/param), the 13B was actually trained on *3\u00d7 more tokens per parameter*, and the \"size advantage\" of the 70B is confounded by the fact that the 13B saw more data per parameter.\n\nThis number is reported in every results table and in the 2\u00d72 mosaic. It does not change the experimental arms, but it changes the *interpretation* of Arm A and Arm B results.\n\n### 4c. Alignment Isolation\n\n- **Arm C** directly computes the alignment delta at each size: \u0394_align_13B = score(13B-chat) \u2212 score(13B-base), \u0394_align_70B = score(70B-chat) \u2212 score(70B-base). The key comparison is the ratio \u0394_align_13B / \u0394_align_70B. If this ratio \u2265 1.0 on Layer 3 tasks, alignment helps the smaller model at least as much, and the size gap on alignment tasks can be closed.\n- **Arm E** tests whether a *different* alignment recipe at 13B scale can close the gap to 70B. This is the most direct test of \"can a lack of refined alignment negate the benefits of a larger parameter count?\"\n\n---\n\n## 5. Analysis Plan\n\n### 6a. Per-Task Metrics\n\nFor each task, each model, the following are computed:\n\n- **Objective tasks (Layers 1\u20132):** accuracy (%) or PPL. One value per model (greedy decoding is deterministic).\n- **Generative tasks (Layer 3):** mean score across 3 seeds, with standard deviation across seeds. The 3-seed SD is the within-model variance.\n\n### 6b. Statistical Tests\n\n**Primary comparison (Arm A): 70B-chat vs 13B-chat**\n\n- For objective tasks: paired comparison on per-problem scores. Compute the paired difference d_i = score_70B(problem_i) \u2212 score_13B(problem_i) for each problem. Report:\n  - Mean of d_i (the point estimate of the size effect)\n  - 95% confidence interval via **10,000-pair bootstrap resampling** of the d_i values\n  - Cohen's d (paired) as the effect size: d = mean(d_i) / SD(d_i)\n  - The bootstrap 95% CI is the primary inferential tool. We do not rely on a single p-value.\n\n- For generative tasks (Layer 3): the comparison is more complex because each (model, problem) pair has 3 seed-level scores. Use a **linear mixed-effects model**:\n  - Fixed effects: model (70B vs 13B), task\n  - Random intercept: problem (to account for repeated measures across models)\n  - Outcome: per-seed score\n  - Report the fixed-effect coefficient for model with 95% CI (profile-likelihood or Wald, whichever is more stable for small n)\n  - If the mixed model is unstable (n_problems < 50 for a given task), fall back to a paired t-test on the 3-seed means per problem, with the 95% CI from the t-distribution.\n\n**Secondary comparisons (Arms B, C, D, E):** same tests, applied to the relevant model pairs.\n\n**Multiple testing correction:** Across the 14 tasks in the battery, apply **Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction** (q = 0.05) to the set of p-values from the primary (Arm A) comparisons. Report both raw and FDR-adjusted CIs. The FDR-corrected result is the one used for the \"necessarily\" conclusion.\n\n### 6c. It is reported with 95% CIs on all coefficients and is interpreted alongside the 2\u00d72 mosaic, not instead of it.\n\n### 6e.
